studies.Reference: Plasma folate, vitamin B6, vitamin B12, homocysteine, and risk of breast cancer.
studies.Authors: Zhang SM, Willett WC, Selhub J, Hunter DJ, Giovannucci EL, Holmes MD, Colditz GA, Hankinson SE
studies.Journal: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Plasma vitamin B(12) levels were measured.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: Blood samples were obtained during 1989 and 1990 from 32 826 women in the Nurses' Health Study who were followed through 1996 for the development of breast cancer. We identified 712 breast cancer case patients and selected 712 individually matched control subjects.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: Plasma vitamin B(12) levels were inversely associated with breast cancer risk among premenopausal women (multivariable RR = 0.36, 95% CI = 0.15 to 0.86 for highest versus lowest quintile).
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: Plasma vitamin B(12) levels were inversely associated with breast cancer risk among premenopausal women.
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: We investigated the association between plasma folate and other vitamins with breast cancer in a prospective, nested case-control study.
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: Plasma vitamin B(12) levels were measured.

headline.funnel_interpretation: The significant funnel plot asymmetry (egger's p=0.0222) indicates substantial publication bias in this meta-analysis on Vitamin B12 and breast cancer. This specific pattern suggests that smaller studies with smaller or null effects may be underrepresented, compromising the reliability of the pooled estimate and potentially leading to an overestimation of the true association.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 9 studies yielded an overall effect size of 0.66 (95% CI: 0.48–0.91), suggesting that Vitamin B12 is associated with a lower risk of breast cancer. However, this association should be interpreted with caution, as there was very high between-study heterogeneity (I² = 87.35%), reflecting highly inconsistent results across studies.
